For $(1+x)^{r}$ , coefficient of $x^{3}$ is $^{r}C_{3}$ So, from $(1+x)^{3}+(1+x)^{4}+\cdot s+(1+x)^{99}$ the total coefficient of $x^{3}$ is $\sum_{99}^{r=3}^{r}C_{3}$ Also, in $(1+kx)^{100}$ , coefficient of $x^{3}$ is $^{100}C_{3}k^{3}$ Hence total coefficient of $x^{3}$ is $\sum_{99}^{r=3}^{r}C_{3}+^{100}C_{3}k^{3}$ Now use the standard NCERT identity: $\sum_{99}^{r=3}^{r}C_{3}=^{100}C_{4}$ So coefficient becomes $^{100}C_{4}+^{100}C_{3}k^{3}$ Given that this equals $(43n+\frac{101}{4})^{100}C_{3}$ Therefore, $^{100}C_{4}+^{100}C_{3}k^{3}=(43n+\frac{101}{4})^{100}C_{3}$ Divide by $^{100}C_{3}$ : $\frac{^{100}C_{4}}{^{100}C_{3}}+k^{3}=43n+\frac{101}{4}$ Now, $\frac{^{100}C_{4}}{^{100}C_{3}}=\frac{100-3}{4}=\frac{97}{4}$ So, $k^{3}+\frac{97}{4}=43n+\frac{101}{4}$ Thus, $k^{3}=43n+1$ We need the smallest $k \in ℕ$ such that $k^{3}-1$ is divisible by $43$ . That is, $k^{3} \equiv 1(mod43)$ Now check smallest natural numbers: $1^{3}=1 \equiv 1(mod43)$ So the smallest value is $k=1$ Hence, $1=43n+1$ which gives $n=0$ But in the question, $n \in ℕ$ . In school-level convention, if $ℕ={0,1,2,\dots}$ , then this is allowed. Thus, $p=1,n=0$ and $p+n=1$ But this is not among the options, so clearly the intended convention is $n \ge 1$ . Now take the smallest $n \in ℕ$ with $n \ge 1$ such that $k^{3}=43n+1$ Try $n=1$ : $k^{3}=44\text{not a cube}$ $n=2$ : $k^{3}=87\text{not a cube}$ $n=3$ : $k^{3}=130\text{not a cube}$ $n=4$ : $k^{3}=173$ $n=5$ : $k^{3}=216=6^{3}$ So smallest such $k$ is $p=6,n=5$ Therefore, $p+n=6+5=11$ Hence the correct answer is: $11$ So, Option B is correct.

questions.question_html: If the coefficients of the middle terms in the binomial expansions of $(1+\alpha x)^{26}$ and $(1-\alpha x)^{28},\alpha \ne 0$ , are equal, then the value of $\alpha$ is:
questions.explanation_text: For a binomial expansion $(a+b)^{n}$ : if $n$ is even, there is only one middle term, and the middle term is the $(\frac{n}{2}+1)$ th term. We are given: $(1+\alpha x)^{26}\text{and}(1-\alpha x)^{28}$ and the coefficients of their middle terms are equal. 1. Middle term of $(1+\alpha x)^{26}$ Since $26$ is even, the middle term is the $(\frac{26}{2}+1)=14$ th term. The general term in $(1+\alpha x)^{26}$ is $T_{r+1}=(\frac{26}{r})(1)^{26-r}(\alpha x)^{r}$ So the $14$ th term corresponds to $r=13$ : $T_{14}=(\frac{26}{13})(\alpha x)^{13}$ Hence, the coefficient of the middle term is $(\frac{26}{13})\alpha^{13}$ 2. Middle term of $(1-\alpha x)^{28}$ Since $28$ is even, the middle term is the $(\frac{28}{2}+1)=15$ th term. The general term is $T_{r+1}=(\frac{28}{r})(1)^{28-r}(-\alpha x)^{r}$ So the $15$ th term corresponds to $r=14$ : $T_{15}=(\frac{28}{14})(-\alpha x)^{14}$ Since $14$ is even, $(-\alpha x)^{14}=\alpha^{14}x^{14}$ Thus, the coefficient of the middle term is $(\frac{28}{14})\alpha^{14}$ 3. Equate the coefficients Given that these coefficients are equal: $(\frac{26}{13})\alpha^{13}=(\frac{28}{14})\alpha^{14}$ Since $\alpha \ne 0$ , divide both sides by $\alpha^{13}$ : $(\frac{26}{13})=(\frac{28}{14})\alpha$ So, $\alpha=\frac{(\frac{26}{13})}{(\frac{28}{14})}$ 4. Simplify $\alpha=\frac{\frac{26!}{13!13!}}{\frac{28!}{14!14!}}$ $\alpha=\frac{26!}{13!13!} \cdot \frac{14!14!}{28!}$ Now use $14!=14 \cdot 13!$ So, $14!14!=(14 \cdot 13!)(14 \cdot 13!)=14^{2}(13!)^{2}$ Thus, $\alpha=\frac{26! \cdot 14^{2}(13!)^{2}}{(13!)^{2} \cdot 28!}=\frac{26! \cdot 14^{2}}{28!}$ Also, $28!=28 \cdot 27 \cdot 26!$ Therefore, $\alpha=\frac{14^{2}}{28 \cdot 27}=\frac{14}{2 \cdot 27}=\frac{7}{27}$ $\alpha=\frac{7}{27}$ So, the correct option is D .
questions.explanation_html:
For a binomial expansion $(a+b)^{n}$ :

  • if $n$ is even, there is only one middle term,

  • and the middle term is the $(\frac{n}{2}+1)$ th term.

We are given:

$(1+\alpha x)^{26}\text{and}(1-\alpha x)^{28}$

and the coefficients of their middle terms are equal.

1. Middle term of $(1+\alpha x)^{26}$

Since $26$ is even, the middle term is the $(\frac{26}{2}+1)=14$ th term.

The general term in $(1+\alpha x)^{26}$ is

$T_{r+1}=(\frac{26}{r})(1)^{26-r}(\alpha x)^{r}$

So the $14$ th term corresponds to $r=13$ :

$T_{14}=(\frac{26}{13})(\alpha x)^{13}$

Hence, the coefficient of the middle term is

$(\frac{26}{13})\alpha^{13}$

2. Middle term of $(1-\alpha x)^{28}$

Since $28$ is even, the middle term is the $(\frac{28}{2}+1)=15$ th term.

The general term is

$T_{r+1}=(\frac{28}{r})(1)^{28-r}(-\alpha x)^{r}$

So the $15$ th term corresponds to $r=14$ :

$T_{15}=(\frac{28}{14})(-\alpha x)^{14}$

Since $14$ is even,

$(-\alpha x)^{14}=\alpha^{14}x^{14}$

Thus, the coefficient of the middle term is

$(\frac{28}{14})\alpha^{14}$

3. Equate the coefficients

Given that these coefficients are equal:

$(\frac{26}{13})\alpha^{13}=(\frac{28}{14})\alpha^{14}$

Since $\alpha \ne 0$ , divide both sides by $\alpha^{13}$ :

$(\frac{26}{13})=(\frac{28}{14})\alpha$

So,

$\alpha=\frac{(\frac{26}{13})}{(\frac{28}{14})}$

4. Simplify

$\alpha=\frac{\frac{26!}{13!13!}}{\frac{28!}{14!14!}}$

$\alpha=\frac{26!}{13!13!} \cdot \frac{14!14!}{28!}$

Now use

$14!=14 \cdot 13!$

So,

$14!14!=(14 \cdot 13!)(14 \cdot 13!)=14^{2}(13!)^{2}$

Thus,

$\alpha=\frac{26! \cdot 14^{2}(13!)^{2}}{(13!)^{2} \cdot 28!}=\frac{26! \cdot 14^{2}}{28!}$

Also,

$28!=28 \cdot 27 \cdot 26!$

Therefore,

$\alpha=\frac{14^{2}}{28 \cdot 27}=\frac{14}{2 \cdot 27}=\frac{7}{27}$

$\alpha=\frac{7}{27}$

So, the correct option is D.

questions.question_html: In the expansion of $(9x-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{x}})^{18},x>0$ , if the term independent of $x$ is (221)k, then k is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: For the expansion of $(9x-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{x}})^{18},$ we use the general term in the binomial expansion: $T_{r+1}=(\frac{18}{r})(9x)^{18-r}(-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{x}})^{r}$ Now simplify the power of $x$ in this term. Since $(9x)^{18-r}=9^{18-r}x^{18-r}$ and $(\frac{1}{3\sqrt{x}})^{r}=\frac{1}{3^{r}x^{r/2}},$ so the power of $x$ in the general term is $x^{18-r-\frac{r}{2}}=x^{18-\frac{3r}{2}}.$ For the term independent of $x$ , the power of $x$ must be zero: $18-\frac{3r}{2}=0$ $\frac{3r}{2}=18$ $r=12$ So the required term is the $(12+1)$ th term, i.e. $T_{13}$ . Now compute it: $T_{13}=(\frac{18}{12})(9x)^{6}(-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{x}})^{12}$ Since the power of $x$ becomes zero, only the numerical coefficient remains: $T_{13}=(\frac{18}{12}) \cdot 9^{6} \cdot \frac{1}{3^{12}}$ Also, $9^{6}=(3^{2})^{6}=3^{12}$ So, $T_{13}=(\frac{18}{12})$ and $(\frac{18}{12})=(\frac{18}{6})=\frac{18!}{6!12!}=18564$ Given that the term independent of $x$ is $(221)k$ , we have $221k=18564$ Thus, $k=\frac{18564}{221}=84$ So the correct answer is: $84$ Hence, Option A is correct.

questions.explanation_html:
Let

$S=(1+x)^{1000}+x(1+x)^{999}+x^{2}(1+x)^{998}+\cdot s+x^{1000}$

Notice that this is a Geometric Progression (GP) with:

  • First term (a): $(1+x)^{1000}$

  • Common ratio $(r):\frac{x}{1+x}$

  • Number of terms ( $n$ ): 1001

The sum of a GP is given by $S=a\frac{(1-r^{n})}{(1-r)}$ . Substituting our values:

$S=(1+x)^{1000}[\frac{1-(\frac{x}{1+x})^{1001}}{1-\frac{x}{1+x}}]$

Simplify the denominator: $1-\frac{x}{1+x}=\frac{1+x-x}{1+x}=\frac{1}{1+x}$ .

$S=(1+x)^{1000} \cdot (1+x)[1-\frac{x^{1001}}{(1+x)^{1001}}]$

$S=(1+x)^{1001}-x^{1001}$

Now we need the coefficients of $x^{499}$ and $x^{500}$ in the simplified expression $(1+x)^{1001}-x^{1001}$ .

Since $x^{1001}$ only affects the term with power 1001, we only look at $(1+x)^{1001}$ .

In the binomial expansion $(1+x)^{n}$

Coefficient of $x^{r}$ is $^{n}C_{r}$

Coefficient of $x^{499}$ in $S$ :

$^{1001}C_{499}$

Coefficient of $x^{500}$ in $S$ :

$^{1001}C_{500}$ (The term $x^{1001}$ does not contribute.)

$\text{Sum of coefficients}$

$\begin{aligned} ^{1001}C_{499}+^{1001}C_{500}=^{1002}C_{500} \end{aligned}$

[ $\text{Using pascal’s identity}$

$^{n}C_{r}+^{n}C_{r+1}=^{n+1}C_{r+1}$ ]

questions.explanation_text: The given expression is $(ax-\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{13}$ So, $\begin{aligned} T_{r+1} & =^{13}C_{r}(ax)^{13-r}(-\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{r} \\ \\ & =^{13}C_{r}(a)^{13-r}x^{13-r-2r}(-1/b)^{r} \\ \\ & =^{13}C_{r}(a)^{13-r}(-\frac{1}{b})^{r}x^{13-3r} \end{aligned}$ For coefficient of $x^{7}$ in $(ax-\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{13}$ $\begin{aligned} & 13-3r=7 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 3r=6 \Rightarrow r=2 \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Coefficient of}x^{7}=^{13}C_{2} \cdot (a)^{11} \cdot \frac{1}{b^{2}} \end{aligned}$ Again, the another expression is $(ax+\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{13}$ So, $T_{n+1}=^{13}C_{r}(ax)^{13-r}(\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{r}=^{13}C_{r}(a)^{13-r}(\frac{1}{b})^{r}x^{13-3r}$ For coefficient $x^{-5}$ in $(ax+\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{13}$ $\begin{aligned} & 13-3r=-5 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow r=6 \end{aligned}$ So, coefficient of $x^{-5}=^{13}C_{6}(a)^{7}\frac{1}{b^{6}}$ Now, according to the question, $^{13}C_{2}(a)^{11}\frac{1}{b^{2}}=^{13}C_{6}(a)^{7}\frac{1}{b^{6}}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow a^{4}b^{4}=\frac{^{13}C_{6}}{^{13}C_{2}} \\ \\ & \therefore a^{4}b^{4}=22 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
The given expression is $(ax-\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{13}$

So,

$\begin{aligned} T_{r+1} & =^{13}C_{r}(ax)^{13-r}(-\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{r} \\ \\ & =^{13}C_{r}(a)^{13-r}x^{13-r-2r}(-1/b)^{r} \\ \\ & =^{13}C_{r}(a)^{13-r}(-\frac{1}{b})^{r}x^{13-3r} \end{aligned}$

For coefficient of $x^{7}$ in $(ax-\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{13}$

$\begin{aligned} & 13-3r=7 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 3r=6 \Rightarrow r=2 \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Coefficient of}x^{7}=^{13}C_{2} \cdot (a)^{11} \cdot \frac{1}{b^{2}} \end{aligned}$

Again, the another expression is $(ax+\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{13}$

So, $T_{n+1}=^{13}C_{r}(ax)^{13-r}(\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{r}=^{13}C_{r}(a)^{13-r}(\frac{1}{b})^{r}x^{13-3r}$

For coefficient $x^{-5}$ in $(ax+\frac{1}{bx^{2}})^{13}$

$\begin{aligned} & 13-3r=-5 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow r=6 \end{aligned}$

So, coefficient of $x^{-5}=^{13}C_{6}(a)^{7}\frac{1}{b^{6}}$

Now, according to the question,

$^{13}C_{2}(a)^{11}\frac{1}{b^{2}}=^{13}C_{6}(a)^{7}\frac{1}{b^{6}}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow a^{4}b^{4}=\frac{^{13}C_{6}}{^{13}C_{2}} \\ \\ & \therefore a^{4}b^{4}=22 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: The coefficient of $x^{n}$ in expansion of $(1+x)(1-x)^{n}$ is
questions.explanation_html:
Given $(1+x)(1-x)^{n}$

= $(1-x)^{n}$ + $x(1-x)^{n}$

General term of $(1-x)^{n}$ = $^{n}C_{r}.(-1)^{r}.x^{r}$

$\therefore$ Term containing $x^{n}$ in $(1-x)^{n}$ = $^{n}C_{n}.(-1)^{n}.x^{n}$

So coefficient of $x^{n}$ in $(1-x)^{n}$ = $^{n}C_{n}.(-1)^{n}$

General term of $x(1-x)^{n}$ = $^{n}C_{r}.(-1)^{r}.x^{r+1}$

$\therefore$ Term containing $x^{n}$ in $x(1-x)^{n}$ = $^{n}C_{n-1}.(-1)^{n-1}.x^{n}$

So coefficient of $x^{n}$ in $x(1-x)^{n}$ = $^{n}C_{n-1}.(-1)^{n-1}$

$\therefore$ coefficient of $x^{n}$ in $(1-x)^{n}$ + $x(1-x)^{n}$

= $^{n}C_{n}.(-1)^{n}$ + $^{n}C_{n-1}.(-1)^{n-1}$

= $(-1)^{n-1}[^{n}C_{n-1}-^{n}C_{n}]$

= $(-1)^{n-1}[n-1]$

= $(-1)^{n}[1-n]$
